summary: Describes how S/MIME version 3 handles certificates, which are used to check that a public key is valid before it is used. It builds on PKIX certificates. It was replaced by RFC 3850.

eli5.summary: Before trusting a name tag, you check it was stamped by someone reliable. This explains how email programs do that check.

subtitle: How S/MIME version 3 uses PKIX certificates to secure email messages and verify senders.

tldr.problem: S/MIME allows secure email through encryption and digital signatures, but email applications need standard ways to handle the certificates that verify those signatures and enable encryption, including checking if certificates are still valid.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME version 3 requires agents (email clients) to use PKIX certificates and to implement specific certificate validation procedures: checking certificate chains back to trusted roots, verifying that certificates have not been revoked using Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), and enforcing constraints and extensions defined in the PKIX standards.
tldr.outcome: Email clients can securely exchange encrypted and signed messages knowing that they can verify the other party's identity through certificate validation, improving trust and security in email communication.

today: RFC 2632 was obsoleted by RFC 3850, which provides an updated version. The fundamental principles of using PKIX certificates, validating certificate chains, and checking revocation remain current practices in secure email.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) provides methods to send and receive encrypted and digitally signed email messages. Before using anyone's public key to encrypt a message or verify a signature, an S/MIME agent (an email client or gateway) must confirm that the public key is legitimate and belongs to that person. This confirmation comes from a certificate—a digitally signed document that binds a public key to an identity.

RFC 2632 specifies how S/MIME version 3 handles certificates. It requires that S/MIME agents use PKIX (Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure) certificates and follow PKIX certificate validation rules, in addition to other requirements specific to email security.
sections.eli5: S/MIME sends secret messages and signs them. Before trusting a signature or using someone's secret code, you need to check that their certificate is real.

sections.title: Certificate Types and Handling
sections.content:
S/MIME version 3 supports PKIX v1 and v3 certificates. These are industry-standard digital certificates defined by the Internet PKI working group. End-entity certificates (those for users and email addresses) MAY contain Internet mail addresses.

The RFC specifies that agents MUST NOT use PKCS #6 extended certificates, an older format, because PKIX extensions provide the same functionality more effectively. Agents SHOULD support X.509 attribute certificates, which can carry additional information about the certificate holder.

When a signed message includes certificates, it often includes a chain: the sender's certificate, the issuer's certificate, the issuer's issuer, and so on up to a root certificate authority. A receiving agent must be able to handle any number of certificates in any order, and should use certificate chaining to build the complete validation path.
sections.eli5: Email uses standard certificates, usually a chain from the sender to a trusted authority. Programs read the whole chain to make sure it's real.

sections.title: Certificate Retrieval and Storage
sections.content:
Email agents need to retrieve certificates for encryption and for verifying signatures. The RFC recommends that agents provide some mechanism to retrieve certificates, such as checking a directory service, looking in DNS, or looking up a user's local address book. Agents may also ask a correspondent for their certificate in a return message.

Receiving agents SHOULD provide a way to store and protect certificates received in incoming messages. This might be a local database or address book that stores each correspondent's certificate. When validating future messages, the agent can check this local store before asking for a fresh copy of the certificate.

Agents SHOULD also provide a mechanism to import and export certificates using special S/MIME messages that carry no content except certificate chains, making it easy to share and backup certificate information.
sections.eli5: Programs should save certificates they receive, so they can look them up again later without asking every time.

sections.title: Email Addresses and Certificate Verification
sections.content:
End-entity certificates for S/MIME SHOULD contain an Internet mail address in the Subject Alternative Name extension (or in the old PKCS #9 emailAddress field). The email address MUST be an RFC 822 address—the standard format for email addresses.

When a receiving agent verifies a signed message, it MUST check that the email address in the From or Sender header matches an Internet mail address in the signer's certificate. If the addresses do not match, the agent SHOULD inform the user explicitly, perhaps showing the addresses from the certificate or other certificate details. This check prevents an attacker from using one person's certificate to impersonate another.

All subject and issuer names in S/MIME-compliant certificates must be populated (non-empty), with one exception: a user's certificate may have an empty subject distinguished name if the subjectAltName extension is marked critical and contains the subject's identifier.
sections.eli5: The email address in the certificate should match the address in the From line. If they do not match, something is wrong.

sections.title: Certificate Chain Validation and Revocation
sections.content:
Before using a certificate, an S/MIME agent must validate the entire certificate chain back to a trusted root certificate authority. Certificate chain validation MUST be performed according to PKIX rules, checking that each certificate is valid, properly signed, and not expired.

Agents MUST support certificate revocation checking using Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs). A CRL is a signed document listing certificates that have been revoked (cancelled) before their normal expiration date. Agents SHOULD check the current CRL every time a certificate is validated, even if it was validated before. Certificates and CRLs received in messages SHOULD be cached and reused for validating subsequent messages.

The RFC identifies key certificate extensions that MUST or SHOULD be supported: Basic Constraints (to indicate if a certificate is a CA), Key Usage (to limit what the key can be used for), and Subject Alternative Name (for email addresses). Key Usage is MUST be marked critical when present.
sections.eli5: Check the whole chain of who signed who, going back to someone you trust. Also check that the certificate hasn't been cancelled by looking at a revocation list.

sections.title: Supported Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
S/MIME version 3 agents MUST be capable of verifying signatures on certificates and CRLs made with the DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) signature algorithm with SHA-1 hashing (id-dsa-with-sha1).

Agents SHOULD be capable of verifying signatures made with RSA encryption combined with MD2, MD5, or SHA-1 hash algorithms (md2WithRSAEncryption, md5WithRSAEncryption, sha-1WithRSAEncryption), with key sizes ranging from 512 bits to 2048 bits.

The differences between the MUST and SHOULD requirements mean that all interoperable S/MIME agents support DSA-SHA1, but not all necessarily support all RSA variants.
sections.eli5: Email programs must understand one way to verify signatures (DSA), and should understand other ways (RSA with different hash algorithms).
